source.title: CopyShield: A Cross-Level Benchmark of Copyright Defenses in LLMs
source.authors: Maryam Alshehyari; Dushyant Singh Chauhan; Samuele Poppi; Martin Takác; S. Lahlou; Nils Lukas

page_placements.theme: Forgetting metrics disagree: output-level forgetting while likelihood, ranks, CoT, paraphrase or facts still carry the target (no attack)

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent cut-off or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: It measures targeted-content leakage and QA utility after copyright defenses, bearing on the suppression-and-utility portion of version A. It does not test whether attacks recover the content after defense.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates copyright suppression, not post-unlearning recovery. It reports no fine-tuning recovery attack, activation-direction ablation, quantization attack, or prompting-only recovery test. Its defense results bear on the initial suppression and utility components of A, but cannot establish whether the suppressed information remains recoverable.
record.test_reason: This benchmark compares copyright-leakage defenses (contrastive decoding, DPO adapter, refusal classifier) on a model fine-tuned to memorize five public-domain books. It measures verbatim and paraphrase leakage plus QA utility. It does not measure targeted-knowledge accuracy against chance. QA knowledge of the books is meant to be kept, not removed. No recovery attack of any kind is run, and the authors leave adversarial extraction to future work. Two of the three defenses are output or refusal filters, not unlearning. This is a related but different construct (copyright output suppression), so the study tests no version. Eldan & Russinovich is cited only in related work.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also conclude that no single defense dominates and that trade-offs depend on model configuration as well as intervention level. DPO's degeneracy is severe on LLaMA (58%) but mild on Mistral (10–14%). They explicitly leave robustness to deliberate extraction attacks to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates copyright defenses: contrastive decoding, DPO trained on task-aware preference pairs, and a hidden-state classifier that blocks responses. It does not reproduce the cited gradient-ascent, Who's Harry Potter, or RMU unlearning recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported trade-offs vary by defense, contrastive-decoding strength, model family, and DPO configuration; DPO QA degeneracy is 58% on LLaMA-3.1-8B and 10% or 14% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 across its two seeds. Activation leakage reduction depends on broad pre-generation blocking.

fits_no_version.finding: DPO nearly eliminates verbatim book continuation (NV-Recall 0.263→0.002 LLaMA; 0.141→0.055 / 0.153→0.052 Mistral). Paraphrase-level reproduction stays at baseline (5.0%→5.5%; 23→22; 20→19 of 200).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preference-trained copyright defenses that suppress verbatim reproduction leave semantic/paraphrase reproduction of the same content intact.

record.problems: The experiments use public-domain books as a proxy for copyrighted material. The LLaMA-3.1-8B experiments use one seed; the authors note that results may vary. Utility relies on a single AI judge and is described as modest. The study does not test post-defense recovery attacks, so its suppression results do not establish whether knowledge was removed or remains recoverable.
record.rows_left_out: QA degeneracy rates and human-rated non-literal quality/risk are not included as separate rows; they are operational or quality outcomes rather than direct measurements of targeted-knowledge recovery. The paper reports them in Sections 6 and Appendix F, Tables 4, 6, 14, and 15.

untested.parts: Not tested: targeted-knowledge accuracy vs chance, unlearning methods (GA/WHP/RMU), and robustness to attacks. Book QA knowledge is deliberately preserved.
No activation-direction ablation or deletion-vs-blocking analysis of an unlearned model.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context attack. Threat model excludes adversarial prompts.
No method is evaluated for resistance to recovery attacks.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to the undefined version 'V1' and labeled A as limits_scope. That is unwarranted: the study measures copyright output leakage, not unlearned-knowledge accuracy, and runs no attacks. Two defenses (contrastive decoding, activation refusal) do not modify weights at all. Reclassified as cites_only/T6; all rows set to none.

versions.untested_parts: The study evaluates leakage reduction and QA utility for copyright defenses. It does not test simple attacks after suppression, nor whether they recover the targeted knowledge; its defenses are not the gradient-ascent, Who's Harry Potter, or RMU methods named in the claim.
No post-defense fine-tuning recovery set is used.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis testing recovery by internal edits is reported.
No quantization attack on defended weights is reported.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context recovery attack is reported.
The study does not evaluate a method's resistance to the recovery attacks in the claim.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Eldan and Russinovich (2023) appears only in a list of behavioural-level defenses and as one row of the Table 1 coverage comparison. The paper does not discuss whether unlearning is shallow or recoverable.

tranche.reason: This is a benchmark of copyright-leakage defenses on a model fine-tuned to memorize five books. It has no targeted-knowledge accuracy measure, QA knowledge is kept on purpose, and it runs no recovery attacks (left to future work). It neither tests nor uses the claim. The reader's earlier T2 was wrong.

source_check.notes: The six checked rows (of 45) match Tables 2, 6 and 15. This study measures copyright leakage (verbatim and embedding-similarity paraphrase), not unlearning robustness. On Mistral, DPO only partly suppresses literal leakage (0.055/0.052 vs 0.141/0.153), and activation intervention suppresses it more.

statements.correction: LLaMA-3.1-8B: NV-Recall 0.263 -> 0.002 (-99.2%; every high-leak sample removed). Mistral-7B-v0.3: 0.141 -> 0.055 (seed 42) and 0.153 -> 0.052 (seed 7), a cut of about 61-66% with residual leakage; activation intervention reaches lower (0.012, 0.006). Non-literal flags: 10 -> 11/200 (5.0% -> 5.5%) LLaMA; 23 -> 22/200 and 20 -> 19/200 Mistral.
statements.problem: All numbers match. But 'nearly eliminates' is true only on LLaMA. The Mistral numbers it cites show about a 61-66% cut with leakage left over, and the paper never calls them near-elimination.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: LLaMA-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and reported Mistral seed 7; measured leakage and QA utility only
reader_labels.reason: Literal and non-literal leakage reductions vary by defense, residual leakage remains for contrastive decoding and DPO, and contrastive decoding lowers QA utility; activation's low leakage involves broad blocking. These results address suppression and utility only, not recovery after attacks (rows r04–r15, r19–r30, r34–r45).
